summary.method: Same prompt, schema, maths and risk checks as the live desk. Point-in-time inputs only. Entry at the first daily close after the news; stops/targets checked on daily closes; round-trip costs charged. Book P&L = R x risk% of book.
summary.caveat: The model may already know how these events played out from its training data, which would flatter these results. Treat this as a test of the machinery and of calibration; the live paper record is the only truly unseen test.

rows.title: Four tankers sabotaged off Fujairah
rows.regime: Event shock with unconfirmed attribution: four tankers sabotaged off Fujairah on 2019-05-12, with no price reaction or base-rate history yet.
rows.noTrade: No trade. The only information is one unsourced breaking headline with no confirmed attribution, no prior incidents in the event study (all base rates n/a), no live vessel data, and no post-news price reaction. Without a historical edge or a verified fact base I cannot put a probability above 0.5 with confidence, and after costs the expected value is not demonstrably positive. I will re-assess once a verified source, a price reaction, or a comparable base rate is available.

rows.title: Front Altair and Kokuka Courageous attacked in the Gulf of Oman
rows.regime: Breaking maritime-risk shock in the Strait of Hormuz / Gulf of Oman, with thin evidence and unclear attribution

trades.thesis: A confirmed attack on two tankers in the Gulf of Oman raises the Persian Gulf supply-disruption premium for several sessions, and Brent had fallen 14.6% over 20 days, so the risk premium had been stripped out.

rows.title: IRGC seizes the tanker Stena Impero in the Strait of Hormuz
rows.regime: Elevated Strait of Hormuz maritime risk after a state seizure, with crude sold off into the news and only a thin prior sample.

trades.thesis: A state seizure in the Strait of Hormuz after a sharp pre-news sell-off should add a short-lived risk premium to front-month Brent over the next week, before the market judges whether the escalation persists.

rows.title: Drone and missile strike on Saudi Abqaiq and Khurais (5.7 mb/d offline)
rows.regime: Supply-shock risk premium in crude after a large Saudi outage, with no post-news price data yet in the input.

trades.thesis: A 5.7 mb/d outage is a large, physical supply loss, so Brent should gap higher on reopening and hold a premium for several sessions while barrels are replaced. The position is closed inside a week because the shipping-family history shows the 20-day move fades.

rows.title: US strike kills IRGC commander Qassem Soleimani
rows.regime: Acute US-Iran military escalation with no post-news price discovery yet; the only prices supplied are pre-strike closes from 2020-01-02.
rows.noTrade: No edge I can state with a calibrated probability: the escalation sample is n=1, the shipping sample is n=3, the entry price is unknown after a gap, and no live vessel data is available (none of the input is marked DEMO, but none is live either). Tanker equities (FRO +20.9%, DHT +17.5% over 20 days) have already re-rated, so chasing them carries asymmetric downside. Revisit after the first post-news sessions, once there are actual Persian Gulf shipping incidents or a clear Iranian retaliation signal.

rows.title: Iran fires missiles at US bases in Iraq
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk spike after the Soleimani strike; no confirmed physical supply disruption yet
rows.noTrade: Thin information: one unconfirmed headline, no evidence of physical damage to Persian Gulf shipping or production, and no vessel data. The escalation sample is n=2 with mixed 5-day and 20-day outcomes, so the base rate does not clear the 0.45-0.65 probability band with a positive after-cost edge. Brent's 1-day move may already price the headline. Revisit if tanker, terminal or Strait of Hormuz disruption is confirmed, or if the follow-up shows Iran widening attacks beyond military bases.

rows.title: Drone strike on the tanker Mercer Street off Oman
rows.regime: Elevated Hormuz maritime risk after a single breaking drone strike on a tanker off Oman; facts still unverified and the market reaction is unknown.
rows.noTrade: Sample too small (shipping family n=3, with mixed 20-day results), the report is a single unverified breaking item, there is no vessel or AIS confirmation, and the post-news price reaction is not in the data, so I cannot put a positive expected value after costs on any allowed instrument.

rows.title: Hamas attack on Israel; regional war risk
rows.regime: Geopolitical headline shock with no confirmed maritime disruption; crude already fell sharply over the prior five sessions.
rows.noTrade: No maritime or supply disruption is confirmed yet, and the Hamas attack is not an attack on shipping or Persian Gulf export infrastructure. The escalation analogues show a positive 1-day Brent median (+3.55%, up 2/3) that fades to a negative 20-day median (-12.21%, up 1/3), and n=3 is too small to set a probability above 0.5 with confidence. Brent (-11.26% over 5 days) and tanker equities have already priced some risk premium. Any expected value I could state would rest on guessed probabilities, not evidence. Re-evaluate on confirmed tanker attacks, Red Sea or Persian Gulf transit disruption, or sustained Brent-WTI or crack-spread dislocation.

rows.title: Houthis seize the car carrier Galaxy Leader in the Red Sea
rows.regime: Red Sea risk re-escalating after a seizure; crude prices were already falling into the event (Brent -12.5% over 20 days), so the risk premium had been largely removed.
rows.noTrade: No crude or product trade: the event is a single car-carrier seizure, the shipping base rate for Brent is weak and n=4, and the 20-day trend already shows risk premium being removed. Only the small FRO long is proposed.

trades.thesis: Continued Red Sea disruption lengthens crude tanker voyages around the Cape, lifting ton-miles and tanker rates; Frontline benefits more than crude prices do.

rows.title: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd pause Red Sea transits; BP follows
rows.regime: Shipping-disruption headline in the Red Sea with no confirmed loss of crude supply; oil prices have already risen 3.5% over five days, and the signal is mainly about container and freight routing.
rows.noTrade: Expected value after costs is not positive under honest probabilities. Brent's 1-day and 5-day shipping-family medians (1.14% and 1.58%) rest on n=5 with 3/5 up, too thin to support a directional edge against a 2.7% daily noise floor. The headline reflects container and freight rerouting, not lost crude barrels, and Brent is already up 3.46% over five days, so part of the move may be priced. Tanker equities (FRO, DHT) show the same thin-sample pattern and high beta, and no live vessel data confirms tanker-specific disruption. Waiting for a confirmed attack on a crude tanker, a seizure, or an official Persian Gulf or Bab el-Mandeb statement would give a clearer analogue and a better base rate.

rows.title: US and UK strike Houthi targets in Yemen
rows.regime: Red Sea conflict escalation after a US/UK strike on Houthi targets; oil and tanker pricing rallied over 20 days but has been flat over 5 days, and the reaction to this specific news is unconfirmed.
rows.noTrade: Event study samples are too small (escalation n=4, shipping n=6) and disagree in direction across horizons: the 1-day Brent up-tilt reverses by 20 days. The 20-day oil and tanker moves already reflect the Red Sea disruption since November, and there is no live AIS or flow data to confirm a new supply disruption. Any edge I could state would be within a few points of 50% and would not clear costs with confidence. Revisit if Brent confirms a move above its recent range on volume, or if vessel-level data shows new Red Sea diversions or attacks on tankers.

rows.title: Houthi missile sets the tanker Marlin Luanda on fire
rows.regime: Red Sea escalation: Houthi strike on a commercial tanker, with Brent already up about 6% over 5 days and headline volatility elevated.

trades.thesis: A direct Houthi strike on a tanker raises the near-term supply-risk premium for crude through Bab el-Mandeb. Historical escalation episodes show a modest 5-day upward drift, though it is not reliable.

rows.title: Iran's drone and missile attack on Israel; IRGC seizes MSC Aries near Hormuz
rows.regime: Acute geopolitical risk spike: Iran-Israel strike plus an IRGC seizure near the Strait of Hormuz, with no price reaction in the data yet and thin historical samples.

trades.thesis: The IRGC seizure of MSC Aries near the Strait of Hormuz and the Iran-Israel strike add a short-lived risk premium that the 04-11 close does not yet reflect, so Brent may rise over the next week before the premium fades.

rows.title: Israeli strike near Isfahan, Iran
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk spike after an unconfirmed Israeli strike near Isfahan, with no shipping-flow confirmation and a weak historical price read.
rows.noTrade: Sample too small (n=6 escalation incidents) and the 1-day Brent pop has faded by day 5 in the historical data, so a directional probability cannot be set meaningfully above 0.5 after costs. The event is an unverified single-source breaking report, and no vessel or AIS data is available to confirm any shipping disruption in the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere. Both sides' official positions are not yet known. Revisit if Brent holds the 1-day gain at the next close, if vessel-tracking data confirms transit disruption, or if the Persian Gulf states or Iran announce concrete shipping measures.

rows.title: Houthis attack the tanker Sounion (1m bbl) in the Red Sea
rows.regime: Event-driven geopolitical risk premium inside a downtrend: Brent is down 4.65% over 5 days and 6.93% over 20 days, so a single attack has to overcome negative momentum.
rows.noTrade: No outright crude or product trade: the 1-day and 5-day Brent medians in the shipping family are near zero with a weak up-count, the 20-day medians are negative, and Brent is in a downtrend. Only a single unverified report is available, with no live vessel data, so the sample is too thin to justify a crude position. The BRENT_WTI, CRACK_321 and GOLD moves in the study are too small to trade on this event.

trades.thesis: A Houthi strike on a crude tanker raises freight and tanker-equity expectations more than it moves crude, which is already weighed down by demand and supply concerns. FRO should keep the 5-day rebound seen in past shipping incidents before fading.

rows.title: Iran fires ~180 ballistic missiles at Israel
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk spike with no confirmed supply disruption; Brent near $73.5 after a fading risk premium
rows.noTrade: No further ideas: no verified supply or shipping disruption, vessel data is unavailable, and the escalation base rates are too thin to support tanker equities or spread trades with positive expected value after costs.

trades.thesis: The strike raises the odds of a wider regional conflict touching Persian Gulf supply, so Brent should carry a short-term risk premium over the next week. The position is small because the premium has already been fading (Brent -2.14% over 5 days).

rows.title: Israel strikes Iran, avoiding oil infrastructure
rows.regime: Geopolitical risk-premium spike with a headline-only, supply-light Israel-Iran strike; no vessel or AIS confirmation available.
rows.noTrade: The only information is a headline that the strike avoided oil infrastructure, which argues against a sustained supply premium. The event-study base rates are weak and small (n=8), with a negative 20-day Brent median and a short-lived 1-5 day bounce that cannot be reliably captured. Tanker equities (FRO, DHT, STNG) have already fallen 7-8% over 5 days, so I see no clean, cost-positive setup and no live AIS confirmation. I will reassess if the strike is followed by confirmed attacks on Persian Gulf or Red Sea shipping or on Iranian export terminals.

rows.title: Israel launches strikes on Iran's nuclear and military sites
rows.regime: Event-driven geopolitical risk spike: Israel's strikes on Iran's nuclear and military sites, with Brent already up about 11.7% over 5 days and 15% over 20 days before the news.
rows.noTrade: No trade. Brent is already up about 11.7% over 5 days and 15% over 20 days, so the initial risk premium is largely in the price. The escalation base rate is weak (BRENT 1d median +0.46, 5d +1.49, 20d -3.32 with only 3 of 9 up), and the input contains no confirmed disruption to Hormuz or Red Sea transits. Tanker equities FRO and DHT moved only about +1.3% and +0.7% over 5 days, so the market is not pricing a shipping shock. Our probability for any directional trade would sit near 0.5, below the cost-adjusted threshold. No live AIS data is available to confirm transit disruption. Revisit if a tanker attack, seizure, or Persian Gulf transit halt is confirmed by an official source.

rows.title: US strikes Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan
rows.regime: Acute state-strike shock on Iran's nuclear sites, with Brent already up about 11% over 5 days and 19% over 20 days before the news.
rows.noTrade: No edge: the event study shows no reliable directional signal for escalation-family headlines (Brent 1-day median 0.07 with 5/10 up; 20-day median -3.55 with 3/10 up), and the pre-news run-up already prices a large premium. No live vessel or AIS data is available, so there is no verified shipping-disruption signal, and the headline is a state strike on nuclear sites rather than an attack on flows. Any directional view would be near 50/50 and would not survive costs.

rows.title: Houthis sink the bulkers Magic Seas and Eternity C
rows.regime: Red Sea escalation headline on a single unverified breaking report; crude price impact so far unclear and historically small for shipping-only incidents
rows.noTrade: Two bulk carriers were reported sunk, but the report is unverified, the vessels are not crude or product tankers, and the point-in-time base rates for shipping and escalation incidents show median moves of well under one standard deviation with up/down splits near 50/50 (Brent 1d +0.53 on 8 samples; escalation Brent 1d -0.33 on 11). Tanker equities (FRO, DHT, STNG) show escalation-family medians of mixed sign and no reliable edge. Without confirmation or a clear price reaction, I cannot state a probability above roughly 0.5 with conviction, so no paper trade is justified. Revisit if the sinking is confirmed by an official source or if tanker rates or Brent move materially on the news.
